transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Well, Doc, I suppose my family's the main reason I'm sitting in this chair today. See, we were all down at the county fair this past weekend—it's a big deal around our parts, you know, everybody brings their best livestock, the newest equipment's all lined up, and I was scheduled to give a talk on soil aeration techniques. I've been farming my whole life, since I was knee-high to a grasshopper, so folks tend to listen when I speak on these things. But... well, right in the middle of it, I just felt this overwhelming need to show them, not just tell them. So I climbed right up onto the big John Deere they had on display. It wasn't even mine, but I got up in the cab and I started jerking the controls around, just pulling levers and turning the wheel, trying to show the crowd this... this 'new pattern' I'd figured out in my head. It made perfect sense to me right then, how the gears and the earth all connect, you know? But my family, they started yelling, the fair organizers were hollering for me to get down, but I just... I couldn't make myself stop. My hands just kept moving, showing them the pattern, even with all that shouting going on. They finally had to come up and pull me out of the seat. So, that's why they drove me here today.
Has anything like this ever happened before, where you felt a sudden, strong need to act on an idea or impulse that others might find unusual?

Well, now, see, that's the thing that's got my wife so worked up. If you look back over the years—and we've been married going on thirty-eight years this October, right around the end of harvest—I've always been what you'd call a steady man. You have to be steady in this line of work, Doc. You can't just go acting on every little notion that pops into your head when you've got two hundred acres of soybeans and a herd of cattle relying on you to do things by the book. The weather's unpredictable enough, you know? You don't need the farmer being unpredictable too. 

So, to answer your question... no, I can't rightly say I've ever had a moment quite like that John Deere situation before. Usually, if I get a new idea about, say, crop rotation or modifying the baler so it doesn't jam up on the wet alfalfa—which it does, constantly, if you don't keep the tension just right on those belts—I'll just sit out on the porch with a cup of coffee and sketch it out on a piece of paper. I don't go making a spectacle. I think things through, step by step. 

That's why it was so strange, I suppose, because it just... it felt so incredibly urgent on Saturday. Like the whole world was waiting for me to show them how the gears align right that very second. But before that? No, I've always just been a regular, nose-to-the-grindstone kind of fella. I wake up at 4:30 AM, I check the fences, I do my work... I certainly don't go climbing on other people's machinery in front of half the county.
After you climbed onto the John Deere and started demonstrating the pattern, how did you feel emotionally? Were you feeling unusually excited, energized, or on top of the world during that time?

Well, Doc, that's a... that's a mighty complicated question, because it's not just about that one moment on the tractor. See, lately, it's like I've been waking up with this... this feeling. Some mornings, I step out onto the porch, coffee in hand, sun just starting to peek over the eastern ridge, and I feel like the whole valley is just... opening up for me. Like the land itself is humming, and I'm grinning at absolutely nothing. Just standing there, grinning like a fool, feeling like I could single-handedly harvest the whole county before noon. I've got this energy bubbling up in my chest, and it feels good, it really does. It feels like I'm finally seeing how everything connects. 

But then... and this is the part that's been causing so much friction at home... if one of the hired hands questions an order I give, or if my wife, Mary—bless her heart, she means well—if she comes out and tells me I need to slow down or come inside and rest, I just... I snap. I mean, I go from feeling like I'm on top of the world to just boiling over with anger. I snap at them like they've just insulted the family name. It's like they're trying to throw a wrench in the gears of this perfect machine I've got running in my head. I've never been a short-tempered man, Doc, you can ask anyone in town. If a calf gets out, I calmly go get it. If the tractor breaks down, I fix it. But lately, when I'm in one of those moods where everything feels so bright and urgent, the slightest little interruption or contradiction just sets me off like a firecracker. And that's exactly how I felt on that John Deere. I felt powerful, I felt like I was showing them the truth of the world, and when they started yelling at me to get down, it just made me so furious. How could they not see it? How could they try to stop me when I was right on the verge of making them understand?

Have you had any periods recently where your mood was unusually high, excited, or irritable for most of the day, nearly every day, lasting several days or more, even if it felt productive or energizing at the time?

Well, Doc, if you're asking about how long this... this whole feeling has been going on, it hasn't just been a passing thing, like a summer squall that blows in and blows out before you can even get the storm windows shut. No, it's been... well, it's been a good long stretch now. For most of this whole time, days on end, I've just been running on that charged, driven feeling I was telling you about. From the moment my boots hit the floorboards in the morning till way past when the owls start hooting. 

I've been making all these big plans, you see. Grand plans for the farm. I figured out this whole new way to re-route the irrigation ditches that would double our yield on the south forty, and I started drawing up schematics for a completely automated feeding system for the cattle—something that would use gravity and a series of counterweights. It all just seemed so clear, so obvious, like I was finally seeing the mechanics of the whole world laid bare. And it wasn't just a day here or a day there. It was day after day after day of this... this incredible, buzzing energy. 

But like I said, it wasn't all just sunshine and productivity. Because for that whole stretch, nearly every single day, if anyone—Mary, the boys, the hired help—if anyone so much as looked at me sideways or told me my ideas were too complicated, or tried to slow me down when I was out there pacing the fields at two in the morning, I'd just snap. I'd bite their heads off. I've been so irritable, so quick to anger, just furious that they couldn't keep up with me or see the vision I had. It's like I've been driving a tractor in high gear with no brakes for days and days, and anyone who steps in the path just gets run over, verbally speaking. So yes, it's been a solid, continuous stretch of feeling like I could conquer the world, and being mad as a hornet at anyone who tried to tell me I couldn't.

Can you think back and tell me if there was a specific time—maybe a few days or even a week—when this feeling of being energized, seeing connections everywhere, and being easily upset was happening most of the time, every day, and really stood out from how you usually feel?

A few days? Or a week? Well, Doc, I... I wish it was just a week. If it was just a week, Mary wouldn't have been nearly so insistent about me coming in to talk to you. See, when you ask for a specific time, it's... it's hard to just point to one week on the calendar. And Mary, she keeps a real strict calendar right there on the kitchen wall by the phone, got all the calving dates and the fertilizer deliveries marked down in red ink so we don't miss a beat. 

If I really sit down and look back over that calendar for the past year or so... well, these charged, sleepless, nonstop stretches, they haven't just been a passing phase. They’ve taken up about ten months of this past year or so. Ten months! I mean, you think about a farmer's year, right? You've got your winter equipment maintenance, your spring planting, summer spraying, fall harvest. And for almost that whole entire cycle, save for maybe a month or two where the engine just kind of sputtered out, I've been running on that high gear. 

Ten whole months out of the last year, just buzzing, seeing all those connections, running on empty but feeling like a million bucks, and getting mad as a wet hen if anyone tried to hit the brakes for me. It's exhausting just thinking about it now, but at the time, day in and day out, month after month... I just couldn't stop. So, no, it wasn't just a specific week that stood out. It's been practically the whole darn year taking over my life.
Have you had any periods recently where you felt down, depressed, or hopeless for most of the day, nearly every day, lasting several days or more?

Down? Depressed? Well, now, Doc, that’s a whole different breed of cat entirely. I mean, you look at some folks around town—like old man Henderson over on the county line, lost his whole winter wheat crop to an early freeze back in '18 and he just sat in his armchair for a month straight, staring at the wall, wouldn't even come out to feed his own dogs. Now that’s what I call depressed. That’s hopeless. But me? No, no, I haven't had anything even close to that. 

I haven't felt low or sluggish or down in the dumps at all. If anything, it's the exact opposite, just like I've been trying to tell you. How can a man feel hopeless when he's got the whole entire world figured out, when the gears in his head are turning so fast and the ideas are just pouring in like a breached dam? Hopeless? Shoot, I feel like I could build a whole new farm from scratch, top to bottom, if you just gave me enough baling wire and a good pair of pliers. 

Mary, she’s even said it herself. She was talking to her sister Brenda on the phone just the other day—I heard her through the kitchen screen door while I was out on the porch fixing the latch that the wind tore up—and she said, "He ain't sad, Brenda, he's just running like a runaway train." And she's right about that part, she really is. I don't wake up feeling heavy or like I can't get out of bed. Lord, no. I wake up way before the sun, practically bouncing off the mattress, ready to get my boots on and make things happen. I haven't had a single day where I just wanted to pull the covers up over my head, not one. 

There's just absolutely no time for feeling down when there's so much work to do, so much I'm seeing out there that nobody else is catching on to yet. You can't be depressed when the land is practically singing to you, you know? So, no, Doc, I wouldn't say I've felt depressed or hopeless. Not for a week, not for a day, not even for a minute. Just... fired up. Always, always fired up.
